title: The {teems} R package user manual
text:
1 Introduction
Reproducibility within computable general equilibrium (CGE) and partial equilibrium modeling analyses has long been elusive, in part due to proprietary data and software. Here we address one aspect of this equation with the introduction of the TEEMS (Trade and Environment Equilibrium Modeling System) open-source software suite.
At its core, TEEMS comprises an R package teems used to compose model runs and teems-solver, a C-based solver capable of solving a large system of nonlinear equations by leveraging a range of mathematical and scientific computation libraries. Auxiliary repositories to facilitate model runs include teems-models, containing internally available and immediately compatible models, and teems-mappings, which contains ready-to-use mappings from coarse to fine resolutions for all core sets in most GTAP-based models.
With a base within the general purpose R scripting language, users are able to seamlessly adjust model components including set aggregations, parameter weighting, closure and shock specifications as well as a large number of options pertaining to the solution and model outputs. Model scripts can then be shared with colleagues, reviewers, and policy-makers for vetting, modification, and reproduction.

title: The {teems} R package user manual
text:
1.1 Motivation
Reproducibility has been elusive also due to the sheer complexity of compiling a single model run. A “simple” model run, for example, broadly involves:

Data and set selection
Set mappings
Model selection
Condensation (backsolving)
Closure selection including any swaps
Shock designation
Set-specific basedata loading, modification, and aggregation
Set- and weight-specific parameter loading, modification, and aggregation
Selection of matrix solution methods
Number of step and subinterval designations
Solution of the nonlinear equation system
Composition of all outputs into structured data

Due to the complexity involved, in the course of building the TEEMS framework we found that in the absence of a reproducible architecture, there is a very high possibility of persistent logic errors propagating through to the output without any obvious indications that this is taking place.
Models which incorporate time steps and additional auxiliary data (e.g., land-use data) or are coupled with other models as is the case with most integrated assessment models (IAMs) are even more complex and thus more susceptible to a wide range of errors.
Ultimately we hope that this software mitigates the steep learning curve requisite to running equilibrium models and allows scientists from various disciplines to advance model representation of their fields. The TL;DR – running a CGE model does not have to be so hard!

title: The {teems} R package user manual
text:
1.2 Errors and model compatibility
This software suite has been under development for many years. Despite our best efforts, it is possible that you will encounter issues – particularly given the wide range of Tablo model files that exist in the field. If your model file does not work, please get in touch and we will seek to expand compatibility.

title: The {teems} R package user manual
text:
1.3 About this manual
This manual is a step-by-step user guide to teems.

title: 2  Dependencies
text:
2.1 Data
This chapter outlines what is needed to run your first CGE model. Ideally all components would be open-source and perhaps one day they will be, but for the moment there are still some minor hurdles to overcome. Before beginning to write model scripts in R with teems, users will need to gain access to a GTAP database and build the teems-solver. GEMPack users can skip the solver step although they will be missing out on a considerable degree of functionality both within the solution process itself and in post-model data availability.
For those skeptical of using R or under the impression that R is only for statistical analysis, we would invite you to investigate speed tests between the R data.table package (widely employed within teems) and comparable packages in Python and Julia. The teems-solver is written in C and uses highly performant Fortran libraries.
The only data currently teems-compatible is available from the Global Trade Analysis Project (GTAP). Although the most recent databases are proprietary, GTAP has consistently made databases available two versions behind the current release: with GTAP 12 current, GTAP 10 is free.
To access the freely available database, users will need to register with GTAP and download the “FlexAgg” format. For GTAP 10 this is accessible under the “GDyn Data Base” entry in the GTAP 10 “Satellite Data and Utilities” section here. For GTAP members that have purchased a database, the current teems version is capable of handling the “FlexAgg” format for GTAP Databases 9 through 12. Models requiring additional headers (e.g., GTAP-EP) require the associated FlexAgg equivalent databases.

title: 2  Dependencies
text:
2.2 R
R (>= 4.3.0) is required. Download and install the latest release for your platform from CRAN.
RStudio is the recommended IDE for working with teems scripts. It provides a script editor, integrated console, and a file browser that makes it straightforward to open, edit, and run the example scripts generated by ems_example(). The 49th Parallel theme with Fira Code font makes for an aesthetically pleasing coding experience.

title: 2  Dependencies
text:
2.3 teems-R package
The R package is available on CRAN.
# install package
install.packages("teems")

title: 2  Dependencies
text:
2.4 teems-solver
teems calls Docker to solve the model’s nonlinear equation system using low-level C and Fortran routines. The solver build is available here: teems-solver. The latest solver build is always compatible with the latest R package version. teems 1.0.0 requires teems-solver 1.1.0 or later and checks the image’s version before every solve: an image built for an earlier release stops with a rebuild message. Rebuild it as described in the teems-solver README (“Updating an Existing Installation”) and restart R.
Two prerequisites:

Docker — install from docker.com. Linux users must also configure Docker to run without sudo.
HSL libraries — the sparse linear algebra packages the solver uses are obtained as a single libHSL source snapshot (libHSL.v2026.8.4.tar.gz) from the STFC licensing portal prior to building. These are available at no cost for academic use.

Two Docker build approaches are available. The expedited build (~5 min) is recommended for most users and uses a pre-built base image containing all open-source dependencies. The full build (~40 min) compiles all dependencies from source.

title: 3  Quickstart
text:
3.1 Generate example scripts
This chapter gets you from a fresh install to a solved CGE model in as few steps as possible, using the freely available GTAP 10 database and the classic GTAP model (version 6.2).
Before continuing, make sure you have completed all prerequisites in the Dependencies chapter:
ems_example() writes a set of ready-to-run R scripts to disk, with your data paths already injected at the top of each file. Point it at your HAR files and a project directory:
paths (the object returned above) is a character vector of file paths to R scripts that are self-contained and immediately runnable.

title: 3  Quickstart
text:
library(teems)

paths <- ems_example(
  model = "GTAPv6",
  path = "~/my_project",
  type = "scripts",
  dat_input = "v6_data/gsddat.har",
  par_input = "v6_data/gsdpar.har",
  set_input = "v6_data/gsdset.har"
)

title: 3  Quickstart
section: 3.2 Step 1: verify the solver with a null run
text:
3.2 Step 1: verify the solver with a null run
Run null.R first. A null run applies no shocks, so every model variable should return zero. Note that the examples below use source() to run a specific script but for interactive runs opening the scripts generated by ems_example() within RStudio is recommended.
source(paths[basename(paths) == "null.R"])

# null.R performs these checks automatically:
check        # TRUE  — all variable values are 0
var_check    # TRUE  — output contains the expected number of variables
coeff_check  # TRUE  — output contains the expected number of coefficients

title: 3  Quickstart
text:
3.3 Step 2: run a uniform shock
full_uniform.R applies a 1% population shock (variable: pop) uniformly across all regions.
source(paths[basename(paths) == "full_uniform.R"])

# full_uniform.R checks that the shock came through:
check  # TRUE — all pop values equal 1 (percentage change)
outputs is a tibble where each row corresponds to a solved variable or coefficient. The dat list column holds the result data for that row in data.table format.
# Inspect results for one variable
outputs$dat$pop
See the Composing results chapter for a full guide to working with outputs.

title: 4  Example files
text:
4.1 Overview
ems_example() writes bundled example model and script files to disk. It is a good starting point for new users, providing ready-to-run material for each of the six vetted models without requiring any additional setup beyond GTAP data access.
Two output modes are available, controlled by the type argument:

title: 4  Example files
text:
"model_files" (default): writes the model (.tab) and closure (.cls) files for the chosen model.
"scripts": writes a complete set of example R scripts covering a range of shock, swap, and solver configurations supported by that model. Each script is a self-contained, runnable workflow from data loading through to result parsing.

ems_example(
  model,
  path,
  type = c("model_files", "scripts"),
  dat_input = NULL,
  par_input = NULL,
  set_input = NULL
)

title: 4  Example files
text:
4.3 Writing model files
The simplest use of ems_example() extracts a model’s Tablo and closure files so they can be inspected or used directly with ems_model() or solve_in_situ().
library(teems)

# Write GTAPv7 model files to a temporary directory
paths <- ems_example("GTAPv7", tempdir())

# Or to a specific directory
paths <- ems_example("GTAP-RE", "~/my_project/model")
The returned list contains two named paths:
paths[["model_file"]]   # path to the .tab file
paths[["closure_file"]] # path to the .cls file
These can be passed directly to ems_model():
model <- ems_model(
  model_file = paths[["model_file"]],
  closure_file = paths[["closure_file"]]
)

title: 4  Example files
text:
4.4 Writing example scripts
When type = "scripts", ems_example() writes a directory of R scripts covering a range of configurations available for the chosen model. Each script is injected with the supplied data paths and is immediately runnable.
paths <- ems_example(
  model = "GTAPv7",
  path = "~/my_project",
  type = "scripts",
  dat_input = "~/dat/GTAP/v12/flexAgg/gsdfdat.har",
  par_input = "~/dat/GTAP/v12/flexAgg/gsdfpar.har",
  set_input = "~/dat/GTAP/v12/flexAgg/gsdfset.har"
)
The GTAP-AEZ scripts need a GTAP-AEZ database (GTAP 11c or newer). The scripts pass the HAR files to ems_data(), which prepares the AEZ layer on load; GTAP_convert(target = "GTAP-AEZ") gives the prepared, unaggregated database in R (see GTAP-AEZ, GTAP-E and GTAP-Power databases):
paths <- ems_example(
  model = "GTAP-AEZ",
  path = "~/my_project",
  type = "scripts",
  dat_input = "~/dat/GTAP-AEZ/v12a/gsdfdat.har",
  par_input = "~/dat/GTAP-AEZ/v12a/gsdfpar.har",
  set_input = "~/dat/GTAP-AEZ/v12a/gsdfset.har"
)
The GTAP-E scripts need a GTAP-E database (GTAP 12a or newer), prepared by ems_data() on load or with GTAP_convert(target = "GTAP-E") (see GTAP-AEZ, GTAP-E and GTAP-Power databases). They aggregate with the energy mapping, which keeps the energy commodities distinct as the model’s nest requires:
paths <- ems_example(
  model = "GTAP-E",
  path = "~/my_project",
  type = "scripts",
  dat_input = "~/dat/GTAP-E/12a/gsdfdat.har",
  par_input = "~/dat/GTAP-E/12a/gsdfpar.har",
  set_input = "~/dat/GTAP-E/12a/gsdfset.har"
)
The GTAP-EP scripts need a GTAP-Power database (GTAP 12a or newer), prepared by ems_data() on load or with GTAP_convert(target = "GTAP-EP") (see GTAP-AEZ, GTAP-E and GTAP-Power databases). They aggregate with the power mapping, which keeps transmission, base load and peak load apart as the generation nest requires:
paths <- ems_example(
  model = "GTAP-EP",
  path = "~/my_project",
  type = "scripts",
  dat_input = "~/dat/GTAP-P/12a/gsdfdat.har",
  par_input = "~/dat/GTAP-P/12a/gsdfpar.har",
  set_input = "~/dat/GTAP-P/12a/gsdfset.har"
)
The data inputs can also be the in-memory list objects returned by GTAP_convert(), which is useful when the raw data needs format conversion before running:
# Convert v7 data to v6.2 format, then generate scripts for the classic model
converted <- GTAP_convert(
  dat_har = "~/dat/GTAP/v12/gsdfdat.har",
  par_har = "~/dat/GTAP/v12/gsdfpar.har",
  set_har = "~/dat/GTAP/v12/gsdfset.har",
  target = "GTAPv6"
)

paths <- ems_example(
  model = "GTAPv6",
  path = "~/my_project",
  type = "scripts",
  dat_input = converted$dat,
  par_input = converted$par,
  set_input = converted$set
)
When list objects are supplied, ems_example() writes data to RDS files alongside the scripts and injects readRDS() calls at the top of each script in place of plain path assignments.

text:
4.5 Using the generated scripts
ems_example() returns a character vector of paths, one per written script. Each script is ready to run; the data paths supplied to ems_example() are injected at the top of the file as plain assignments.

4.5.1 Script naming convention
Script file names encode the shock and swap configuration (the exact set varies by model):



File name
What it demonstrates

numeraire.R
Uniform shock to the numeraire (pfactwld): all prices move by the shock and real variables stay unchanged


full_uniform.R
Uniform shock across all elements of a variable


part_uniform.R
Uniform shock on a subset of elements


part_uniform_full_swap.R
Partial shock plus a full-variable closure swap


part_uniform_part_swap.R
Partial shock plus a partial closure swap


part_uniform_part_swap_mixed.R
Partial shock plus mixed (full + partial) swaps


part_uniform_subset_swap.R
Partial shock and swaps with mixed multiple elements and subsets


custom_full.R
Heterogeneous shock values supplied as a data frame

Heterogeneous shock values supplied as a data frame on a subset of elements


custom_full_csv.R

4.5.2 Structure of a generated script
Each script begins with the injected assignments followed by the template body. Opening part_uniform.R in an editor shows:
dat_input = "~/dat/GTAP/v12/flexAgg/gsdfdat.har"
par_input = "~/dat/GTAP/v12/flexAgg/gsdfpar.har"
set_input = "~/dat/GTAP/v12/flexAgg/gsdfset.har"
model_file = "~/my_project/GTAP-RE.tab"
closure_file = "~/my_project/GTAP-RE.cls"

dat <- ems_data(
  dat_input = dat_input,
  par_input = par_input,
  set_input = set_input,
  time_steps = c(0, 1, 2),
  REG = "big3",
  ACTS = "macro_sector",
  ENDW = "labor_agg"
)

model <- ems_model(
  model_file = model_file,
  closure_file = closure_file
)

partial <- ems_uniform_shock(
  var = "aoall",
  value = -1,
  REGr = "chn",
  ACTSa = "crops"
)

cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  shock = partial
)

outputs <- ems_solve(
  cmf_path = cmf_path,
  matrix_method = "SBBD",
  n_tasks = 2L,
  solution_method = "Gragg"
)

title: 4  Example files
text:
4.6 Output
ems_example() returns a character vector of file paths to the written files. For type = "model_files" this is the .tab and .cls paths. For type = "scripts" this is one path per written script.

title: 5  Loading and specifying sets
text:
5.1 Overview
Set mappings aggregate the granular regions, sectors, and endowments in the GTAP database to the resolution desired for a given model run. In ems_data(), these are passed as named arguments via ..., where each argument name corresponds to a set name in the model Tablo file.
Any set provided with a mapping is treated as a parent mapping and aggregated accordingly. Sets not explicitly mapped are handled automatically: if a set’s elements are a subset of a mapped set’s elements, the parent mapping is inherited; if a set’s elements span multiple mapped sets, the relevant portion of each parent mapping is applied. If a set has no element-level relationship to any mapped set, it remains unaggregated.
For the base GTAP models the minimum required mappings are:
All other read-in sets (e.g. MARG_COMM in GTAPv6.2, MARG in GTAPv7) are derived automatically from the parent mapping. Additional mappings can always be supplied explicitly to override the inferred result.

title: 5  Loading and specifying sets
text:
5.3 External mappings
Custom mappings can be provided as a file path to a two-column CSV or a data frame (e.g., data.table or tibble), where the first column contains origin elements and the second column contains destination (aggregated) elements. See teems-mappings for example files. Set element names are case-insensitive on input and lowercase everywhere else: the elements a database ships (Land, NatlRes, CGDS), the origin and destination columns of a mapping, and the elements named in shocks, swaps and closures are all folded to lowercase, and every TEEMS object and solver output carries them in lowercase.
v7_data <- ems_data(dat_input = "v7_data/gsdfdat.har",
                    par_input = "v7_data/gsdfpar.har",
                    set_input = "v7_data/gsdfset.har",
                    REG = "path/to/custom_REG_mapping.csv",  # external mapping
                    ACTS = "macro_sector",
                    ENDW = "labor_agg"
)

title: 6  Loading data
text:
6.1 Overview
The ems_data() function loads and prepares GTAP database files for use in CGE model runs. It handles the three core GTAP data files (dat, par, and set) and is also used to specify any time steps (for temporally dynamic models) and load set mappings for sets that are read into the model (i.e., not constructed from set operations).
GTAP databases need all three input files (dat_input, par_input, set_input) and the model-specific set mappings; a database held in a single HAR file needs dat_input alone (see below). time_steps is required for intertemporal models.

title: 6  Loading data
text:
6.2 Input files
Compatible input files are currently limited to those produced by the Global Trade Analysis Project (GTAP). Although the most recent database releases are proprietary, GTAP has consistently made databases publicly available two versions behind the current release: with GTAP 12 current, GTAP 10 is free.
In order to access the freely available database, users will need to register with GTAP and download the “FlexAgg” format. For GTAP 10 this is accessible under the “GDyn Data Base” entry in the GTAP 10 “Satellite Data and Utilities” section here. For paying GTAP members, the current teems version is capable of handling the “FlexAgg” format for GTAP Databases 9 through 12.
The following command will load data consistent with the standard GTAP model, using broad aggregations for regions, commodities, and endowments. Users will need to specify the location of data ("v7_data/gsdfdat.har" placeholder).
v7_data <- ems_data(dat_input = "v7_data/gsdfdat.har", # basedata coefficients
                    par_input = "v7_data/gsdfpar.har", # parameter coefficients
                    set_input = "v7_data/gsdfset.har", # set elements
                    REG = "big3",
                    ACTS = "macro_sector",
                    ENDW = "labor_diff"
)
Note that the actual names of HAR data files vary according to the GTAP release.
A database held in a single HAR file, such as the ORANI-G basedata.har, is loaded by giving dat_input alone. Every character header with distinct entries becomes a set named after its header, every real header a coefficient dimensioned by the set labels stored in the file, and the data are passed through at full resolution; set mappings do not apply on this route.
orani_data <- ems_data(dat_input = "oranig/basedata.har")
Sets read this way keep the element order of their header in the file; so does any set passed through without aggregation on the GTAP route. Aggregated sets are ordered by their mapping. The order matters to a model that works by position, for example through $POS or a mapping read from a header.
A real header stored without set labels is laid out over the sets declared by the coefficient that reads it, in the file’s storage order. If the header’s size or shape does not fit that declaration, ems_deploy() stops with an error naming the header and the coefficient.

title: 6  Loading data
text:
6.3 Set mappings
Set mappings aggregate the fine-grained regions, sectors, and endowments in the GTAP database down to the resolution required for a given model run. The set names used in ... depend on the data format — see the Loading and specifying sets chapter for the full list of internal mappings and instructions for supplying custom CSV mappings.

title: 6  Loading data
text:
6.4 Time steps
For temporally dynamic models (e.g., GTAP-RE), time steps must be provided representing t0 plus actual year steps from t0. Time steps can be inputted in either actual year increments or represented as chronological years. Note that if chronological years are used, t0 must correspond with the reference year of the database being used.
The following uses explicit time steps (steps from t0), equivalent to chronological years c(2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2023, 2025, 2027, 2029, 2031, 2033) for a database with a 2017 reference year.
data <- ems_data(dat_input = "v7_data/gsdfdat.har",
                 par_input = "v7_data/gsdfpar.har",
                 set_input = "v7_data/gsdfset.har",
                 time_steps = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16),
                 REG = "WB23",
                 ACTS = "services",
                 ENDW = "labor_agg"
)
Chronological time steps (with t0 corresponding to the reference year of input data).
data <- ems_data(dat_input = "v7_data/gsdfdat.har",
                 par_input = "v7_data/gsdfpar.har",
                 set_input = "v7_data/gsdfset.har",

The returned list can be passed directly to ems_data() or ems_example(). After a conversion, set mappings are specified for the target format, not the original format of the data.

  par_har = "v7_data/gsdfpar.har",
  set_har = "v7_data/gsdfset.har",
  target = "GTAPv6"
)

                    par_input = converted$par,
                    set_input = converted$set,
                    REG = "big3",
                    PROD_COMM = "macro_sector",
                    ENDW_COMM = "labor_agg"
)

  dat_har = "v6_data/gsddat.har",
  par_har = "v6_data/gsdpar.har",
  set_har = "v6_data/gsdset.har",
  target = "GTAPv7"

                    par_input = converted$par,
                    set_input = converted$set,
                    REG = "AR5",
                    ACTS = "macro_sector",
                    ENDW = "labor_agg"
)


6.5.3 GTAP-AEZ, GTAP-E and GTAP-Power databases
The GTAP-AEZ, GTAP-E and GTAP-EP models read sets and parameters that their databases do not ship in the form the model expects. ems_data() recognises these databases and prepares them on load, so the HAR files can be passed directly. To work with a prepared database in R before aggregation, use GTAP_convert() with target = "GTAP-AEZ", "GTAP-E" or "GTAP-EP"; this prepares the database (generates new headers) but does not convert its format. Conversion between v6 and v7 versions of these databases is not supported.

                   par_input = "e_data/gsdfpar.har",
                   set_input = "e_data/gsdfset.har",
                   REG = "big3",
                   ACTS = "energy"
)

title: 6  Loading data
text:
6.6 Data aggregation
Data is aggregated according to type, with non-parameter coefficients summed by target set mappings and weighted averages calculated for the parameters below. A simple mean is applied to parameters not listed below, and to the two base data headers that are not values: DPSM (the sum of the household distribution parameters, 1 in every region) and, in GTAP-E and GTAP-Power data, GSHR (the government share of carbon tax revenue). If custom parameter values are desired, these can be directly loaded in their final format into the ems_model() function, and no aggregation or modification will take place. In the below notation, hat (ˆ) indicates the new parameter value and asterisk indicates the destination set mapping.

6.6.1 Parameter weights
The elasticities are aggregated region by region under the share method, so each aggregated region keeps its own values; the value method follows FlexAgg, which weights the Armington, intermediate-input and value-added elasticities (ESBD, ESBM, ESDC, ESMC, ESBC, ESBV) with world totals and writes one value to every region. Two weighting methods are available through the par_weights argument of ems_data():

"value" (default): each member is weighted by the value of its nest, as the GTAP aggregation programs (FlexAgg) do; the formulas are given below. The region-generic parameters (ESBD, ESBM, ESDC, ESMC, ESBC, ESBV) are weighted with world totals and take one value in every region, as FlexAgg writes them; a parameter file that carries them region-specific is first averaged over regions with the same weights.
"share": each member is weighted by the value of its CES or CET nest, \(V\), times one minus the sum of its squared input shares \(\theta_k\), \[
w = V\left(1 - \sum_k \theta_k^2\right).
\] This is the weight under which the aggregate elasticity reproduces the members’ response to a small change in relative prices. A member whose input shares cannot move carries little weight: a commodity that is almost never imported cannot shift the aggregate import share, whatever its elasticity, and neither can imports bought almost entirely from one source. For a nest with two inputs the weight reduces to \(2 V \theta (1 - \theta)\). Shares are taken over the inputs of the aggregated model (for import sourcing, the aggregated source regions). Where every member of an aggregate has a zero weight, the value weight is used instead; where that is zero too (an activity or endowment a region does not have), the members are averaged. Where such members dominate an aggregate, as oil and gas do in the mining sector of an importing region, the share-weighted elasticity can fall far below the value-weighted one.

A single method applies to every weighted parameter; individual parameters can be set apart by name:
v7_data <- ems_data("v7_data/gsdfdat.har",
                    "v7_data/gsdfpar.har",
                    "v7_data/gsdfset.har",
                    REG = "big3",
                    ACTS = "macro_sector",
                    ENDW = "labor_agg",
                    par_weights = c(ESBM = "share"))

The layer parameters are averaged, except for the following.
The elasticity of substitution between value added and energy, \(\sigma_\text{vae}\) (EFVE), is weighted by the share weight of the value-added/energy nest ("share") or by the value of primary factors and energy inputs ("value"), where \(g\) runs over the energy commodities (COME):
\[
\hat{\sigma}_{\text{vae}_{a,r}} = \frac{\sum_{a,r}^{a^{*}r^{*}}\sigma_{\text{vae}_{a,r}}\,vaen_{a,r}}{\sum_{a,r}^{a^{*}r^{*}} vaen_{a,r}},
\qquad
vaen_{a,r} = \sum_{e} evfp_{e,a,r} + \sum_{g} (vdfp_{g,a,r} + vmfp_{g,a,r})
\tag{6.16}\]
For the fossil fuel mining activities (coal, oil and gas) it is instead recalibrated at the aggregate level so that the activity reproduces the target supply elasticity \(\eta\) (SPLY, averaged over all regions), given the cost shares of natural resources (\(s_\text{nr}\)) and of \(vaen\) (\(s_\text{vaen}\)) in the value of output, assuming, as Burniaux and Truong (2002) do, a Leontief top nest and perfectly elastic supply of every input other than the natural resource:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_{\text{vae}_{a,r}} = \frac{\eta_{a}}{1/s_{\text{nr}_{a,r}} - 1/s_{\text{vaen}_{a,r}}}
\tag{6.17}\]
The other fuels (p_c, gdt) take \(\hat{\sigma}_\text{vae} = 1\).
The elasticity of substitution between land in different agro-ecological zones, \(\sigma_\text{aez}\) (EAEZ), is weighted by land rents, the primary factor purchases \(evfp_{e,a,r}\) over the zones \(e \in\) AEZS ("value"), or by their share weight across zones ("share").

title: 7  Loading models
text:
7.3 Closure selection
Standard model-specific closures are available within the model repository: teems-models. The general format consists of an exogenous block listing all (\n delimited) exogenous variables, followed by ;, rest endogenous, and ; to mark the end:
exogenous
pop
aoreg("row")
qe(ENDWC,REG,INITIME)
txs(MARG,"row",REG,FWDTIME)
...
;
rest endogenous
;
Each entry is either a full variable name (pop), an entry with specific set elements (aoreg("row")), a mixed entry (txs(MARG,"chn",REG,FWDTIME)) or an entry with subsets (qe(ENDWC,REG,INITIME)).

title: 7  Loading models
text:
7.4 Tablo compatibility
The teems-solver follows GEMPACK’s Tablo language, so most model files written for GEMPACK load as they are. This manual will not attempt to reproduce the very thorough GEMPACK documentation, rather lists what is supported and the few forms that are not. ems_model() checks the model file before anything is solved. Problems are reported by name, with the statement it occurs in, rather than surfacing later as a solver failure. If a model file does not load and you think it should, a supported statement behavior is not as expected, or an error propagates to the solver without warning, please get in touch.

7.4.1 Supported statements
File, Coefficient, Read, Update, Set, Subset, Mapping, Formula, Assertion, Variable, Equation, Write, Zerodivide, Complementarity, Loop with Break and Cycle, PostSim sections, and the condensation statements Substitute and Backsolve (see Condensation) are accepted. Omit statements hold the omitted variables exogenous and unshocked, as omission does in GEMPACK; they stay in the model and its outputs. Levels variables and equations, Formula & Equation, and Read (IfHeaderExists) are supported; levels equations may contain conditional sums, PROD and the functions SQRT, EXP, LOGE, LOG10 and IF. PROD, MAXS and MINS reduce over a set like SUM. Default statements (Variable (Default=Levels);, Equation (Default=Levels);, Formula (Default=Initial);, Coefficient (Default=Parameter);) apply to the statements that follow them. Read, Formula and Assertion statements take effect in the order they appear, including inside PostSim sections: a Read after a default Formula replaces the default, and a Formula after a Read replaces what was read. A levels variable X has a linear variable named p_X, or c_X for a (change) variable; Linear_Name= gives it another name and Linear_Var= makes an already declared linear variable serve as it. In closures, shocks and swaps either name may be used. p_X and c_X refer to nothing else: beside a linear variable X, names such as p_X or C_X are free for other coefficients and variables.
Display and Transfer are not supported and raise an error: every coefficient is in the coefficient dump, and TEEMS writes no Header Array output files.


7.4.2 Names
Names are case-insensitive. A set, coefficient, variable, file or equation may be written in any case after its declaration, and TEEMS uses the declared spelling throughout, including in outputs. The same holds for header names (Read ... header "Nat" finds a header NAT), logical file names, the .tab and .har extensions, and the variable, set and element names in closures, shocks and swaps.


7.4.3 Variable types for homogeneity checks
VPQType marks a variable as a Value, Price or Quantity, or as None (tax rates, shifters, technology, foreign prices), for homogeneity tests (GEMPACK manual 57.2). All three GEMPACK forms are read, in file order:
Variable (begins p default VPQType Price);  ! later variables starting with p !
Variable (begins pf default VPQType None);  ! the longest matching prefix wins !
Variable (VPQType=Quantity) (all,i,IND) x1cap(i);
Variable (Name x6com VPQType Quantity);     ! anywhere in the file !
Variable (begins <prefix> VPQType default OFF); ends a default. Variables without a type stay Unspecified. ORIG_LEVEL= qualifiers are checked: the coefficient must be real and range over exactly the variable’s sets.


7.4.4 Formulas, updates and mappings

Formula quantifiers may carry general conditions, such as (all,c,COM: $POS(c) = $POS(g)), a coefficient on either side, or a mapping (MAP(z) = r). Update statements take quantifier conditions too; an element whose condition is false is left unchanged.
A qualifier list such as (initial, by_elements) is accepted. write updated value to file is accepted with a warning but writes no separate file; the value is in the coefficient outputs.
An index may be repeated within one reference (T(d,d), TRADE(c,"dom",r,r)).
A mapping may point into a subset of the set its argument position is declared over, and a mapped index may range over a subset of the mapping’s domain. A mapping may also be assigned an identity or a copy (MAP(c) = c, A(z) = B(z)), matched by element name when the sets are unrelated.
A mapping is read as element names (Read (by_elements)) or as element numbers (Read alone), over its whole domain or over a subset (Read (all,c,MARG) MAP(c) ...), with Formulas assigning the rest.
Update statements read the values at the start of each step, and several updates of one element apply in order, the later overriding. (change) and (explicit) updated data follow the solution path and are extrapolated like the variables; see single-pass runs for models where that is not wanted.



7.4.5 Sets
Sets may be read from file, listed explicitly, or built from other sets:
Set A123 = A1 + A2 + A3;
Set B = (C - D) INTERSECT E;
Set B2 # equal to A # = A;
Set UACT = UNITA x ACTS;
Set COALCOMM # coal # =
    (all,c,COMM: sum{cc,DCOMM: MCOM(cc)=c, UNITDCOAL(cc)} > 0);
Set expressions (UNION, INTERSECT, +, -, and the relative complement \), set equality, set products and conditional set builders are supported. A few points to note:

A set must not be named union or intersect.
A conditional set builder, like COALCOMM above, compares an expression with a constant. Its source set may be read, listed or itself built from other sets. Sets are built before the model is solved, so the condition is evaluated at deployment from the loaded data: the coefficients in it must be read from a file or assigned by Formula statements that precede the Set statement and use only what is known by then (arithmetic, IF, sums, the standard functions); RANDOM cannot appear. GTAP-E’s UNITDCOAL(c) = 0.0 + IF[c="coa", 1.0] is such a formula.
Some GTAP models build sets from the EFLG and SLUG headers, which TEEMS excludes from the data. Declare such sets with explicit elements instead.
Intertemporal set equality (Set (Intertemporal) B = A;) is not supported.
A set may be empty, for example when a conditional set builder selects nothing under the data at hand. Statements over an empty set do nothing and sums over it are zero.

Set element names are lowercase throughout TEEMS (see Set mappings); for example, the v6.2 CGDS sector becomes cgds.
Element order follows the data file wherever a set is not aggregated (see Loading data). It matters to anything that works by position, such as $POS and a mapping read from a header, whose entries line up with the elements of its domain in order.


7.4.6 IF conditions
IF[condition, expression] is supported wherever an expression may stand, in formulas, updates, assertions, PostSim statements and linear or levels equations:
Formula (all,c,COMM)(all,r,REG)
    VCB(c,r) = VDB(c,r) + sum{d,REG, VXSB(c,r,d)} + IF[c in MARG, VST(c,r)];
Equation E_qca (all,c,COMM)(all,a,ACTS)(all,r,REG)
    qca(c,a,r) = IF[MAKES(c,a,r) gt 0,
                    qo(a,r) - ETRAQ(a,r) * [ps(c,a,r) - po(a,r)]];
Formula (all,r,REG) SHR(r) = sum{s,REG, IF[s <> r, VDB("food",s)]} / 2;
A condition may test set membership (c in MARG), compare an index with an element or another index (d = "domestic", r <> s), or compare coefficient expressions (MAKES(c,a,r) gt 0). Comparisons may be joined with AND, OR and NOT ([VDB(c,r) > 0] and not [r = "usa"]), in IF terms as in the conditions of sums and quantifiers. IF terms may be nested, multiplied, divided, raised to powers, placed inside sums and function arguments, and used in formulas without quantifiers (Formula D = 0.0 + IF[NM > 1, 1];). Top-level terms of formulas and equations are rewritten at model load into equivalent unconditional statements, with helper coefficients and sets (named IFC*, IFX*, IFT*, IFV*, IFO*) that appear in outputs like any other coefficient or set; other placements are evaluated by the solver as written.
A condition reads coefficients and levels variables but not linear variables, and a set-membership test (c in MARG) cannot be combined with AND, OR or NOT; nest the IF instead.

title: 7  Loading models
text:
7.5 Condensation
Condensation makes the system passed to the solver smaller without changing the model’s economics. TEEMS condenses by backsolving variables.
The static vetted models come condensed. The GTAPv6, GTAPv7, GTAP-AEZ, GTAP-E and GTAP-EP model files carry the standard GTAP backsolves as Backsolve statements, and ORANI-G its own; ems_model() applies them on load. GTAP-RE carries none, because backsolving slows the parallel methods intertemporal models use (see below). To solve the full system, load a model with ignore_condense = TRUE.

7.5.1 Backsolving variables
A backsolved variable is substituted out of the system using its defining equation and recovered by the solver after each step, so it still appears in the outputs. By default the defining equation is E_<variable>; name it explicitly when it differs:
model <- ems_model(
  model_file = GTAPv7[["model_file"]],
  closure_file = GTAPv7[["closure_file"]],
  backsolve = c("pfd", "pfm", ps = "E_ps")
)
A backsolved variable must be endogenous, and its defining equation must be one GEMPACK could substitute with. If it is not, the error names the requirement that failed. #### Condensation coefficients (CSUB) {#csub}
Substituting a variable out multiplies the coefficients of its defining equation into every equation that used it. Rather than leave those products in the equation text, the engine stores each one, and each sum over an eliminated index, as a new coefficient with its own Formula, named CSUB<n> and appended to the deployed model file. Substituting pint out of GTAPv7 through E_pint, for example, produces
Coefficient (all,a,ACTS)(all,r,REG)(all,c,COMM)
    CSUB392(a,r,c) # backsolve product (E_pint) #;
Formula (all,a,ACTS)(all,r,REG)(all,c,COMM)
    CSUB392(a,r,c) = INTSHR(c,a,r)*[1 - FMSHR(c,a,r)];
and later substitutions build on earlier ones:
CSUB204(r,c) = sum{a,ACTS, CSUB53(r,c,a)*CSUB174(c,a,r)}
The comment names the kind: a backsolve product is such a product or sum; a backsolve pivot is the reciprocal of the coefficient on the backsolved variable when that coefficient is not a plain number.
They are derived from the model’s coefficients, not declared by it, and are re-evaluated with the other formulas at every step. The standard GTAPv7 condensation adds 650 of them to the 283 coefficients the model declares, so the solver’s write tally (verbosity = 2) reports the two groups separately. ems_compose() leaves them out of the default outputs and returns one only when it is named in which, and write_coefficients = TRUE writes no CSV for them.


7.5.2 When backsolving pays
Backsolving shrinks the system but makes it denser. That helps "LU" on static models: the standard GTAP condensation cut a 1.35 million equation Gragg solve by 41 % and a 3.6 million one by more than half. It hurts the parallel matrix methods ("SBBD", "DBBD", "NDBBD"), which rely on the sparsity it removes: on GTAP-RE the same condensation made "SBBD" runs 69 % slower at 200 thousand equations and 393 % slower at 4.4 million, and a condensed static system stops gaining from extra "DBBD" tasks where the full system keeps gaining. On a laptop, threaded "LU" on the condensed system is still the fastest measured below about 120 thousand condensed equations; above that, or on a machine with many cores, deploy without backsolve and use a parallel method. ems_probe() measures the block structure of a deployment and suggests which case it is likely in.


7.5.3 Condensation statements in the model file
Substitute and Backsolve statements in a model file are applied on load:
Substitute p1 using E_p1 ;
Backsolve p1lab using E_p1lab ;
Substitute is carried out as a backsolve, so the variable stays in the outputs. Statements in the file are applied first, then the backsolve argument. ignore_condense = TRUE skips the statements in the file but still applies the argument.
Omit statements add the listed variables to the closure as exogenous, unshocked entries, with a message. They stay in the model and its outputs, so a closure file need not repeat them.
Closure files may also carry xSet and xSubset lines as written in a GEMPACK command file; they are read as Set and Subset statements of the model, so closure entries can refer to them.

title: 7  Loading models
text:
7.6 Coefficient value injection
The ... argument in ems_model() allows users to assign aggregation-specific values to model coefficients. This is used to inject modified values into existing coefficients as well as provide data to new coefficients. All data inputted here must be model-aggregation specific and will not be subject to aggregation. The left-hand side (name) must correspond to a coefficient (not header) declared within the model input. Data frame and CSV inputs are validated against the set aggregations from ems_data(). Dimensions must match the aggregated resolution, not the original database resolution. Three input types are supported, with model “Read” and “Formula” declarations modified accordingly:

7.6.1 Uniform numeric value
A single numeric value can be assigned to a coefficient. All set combinations for that coefficient will receive this uniform value.
GTAP_RE <- ems_example("GTAP-RE", tempdir())
model <- ems_model(
  model_file = GTAP_RE[["model_file"]],
  closure_file = GTAP_RE[["closure_file"]],
  KAPPA = 0.54321
)
Providing a numeric vector of length greater than 1 will raise an error. Instead here use a data frame with the appropriate sets to assign multiple heterogeneous values to a coefficient.


7.6.2 Data frame
A data frame (or data frame extension such as tibble or data.table) can be used to assign heterogeneous values across set combinations. The data frame must contain columns for each set index using the model-specific naming convention (set name + variable index, e.g., REGr, COMMc, ALLTIMEt) and a Value column.
# Heterogeneous values for SUBPAR coefficient (Read-type)
GTAP_RE <- ems_example("GTAP-RE", tempdir())
COMMc <- c("crops", "food", "livestock", "mnfcs", "svces")
REGr <- c("usa", "chn", "row")
ALLTIMEt <- seq(0, 10)

SUBPAR <- expand.grid(
  COMMc = COMMc,
  REGr = REGr,
  ALLTIMEt = ALLTIMEt
)

SUBPAR$Value <- runif(nrow(SUBPAR))

model <- ems_model(
  model_file = GTAP_RE[["model_file"]],
  closure_file = GTAP_RE[["closure_file"]],
  SUBPAR = SUBPAR
)
This works for both Read-type and Formula-type coefficients:
# Heterogeneous values for CPHI coefficient (Formula-type)
REGr <- c("usa", "chn", "row")
ALLTIMEt <- seq(0, 10)

CPHI <- expand.grid(
  REGr = REGr,
  ALLTIMEt = ALLTIMEt
)
CPHI$Value <- runif(nrow(CPHI))

model <- ems_model(
  model_file = GTAP_RE[["model_file"]],
  closure_file = GTAP_RE[["closure_file"]],
  CPHI = CPHI
)


7.6.3 CSV file
A path to a CSV file can be used as an alternative to a data frame. The CSV must follow the same structure: set index columns and a Value column.
# Write coefficient data to CSV
write.csv(SUBPAR, "SUBPAR.csv", row.names = FALSE)

model <- ems_model(
  model_file = GTAP_RE[["model_file"]],
  closure_file = GTAP_RE[["closure_file"]],
  SUBPAR = "SUBPAR.csv"
)


7.6.4 Combining injections
Multiple coefficient injections can be combined in a single call:
model <- ems_model(
  model_file = GTAP_RE[["model_file"]],
  closure_file = GTAP_RE[["closure_file"]],
  KAPPA = 0.03,
  SUBPAR = SUBPAR,
  CPHI = CPHI
)
If the coefficient name is not found in the model, an error is raised indicating that the aggregated data coefficient is not declared within the provided model input.

title: 7  Loading models
text:
7.7 Intertemporal models
For intertemporal models, ems_model() determines temporal dynamics by detecting intertemporal sets in the Tablo file. By default, the expected header in the GTAP-RE model is "YEAR". If a model uses a different header for timestep data, set it via ems_option_set():
ems_option_set(timestep_header = "AYRS")
If the expected timestep header is not found in the model, an error will be raised with a suggestion to use ems_option_set() to configure a custom timestep header. The same concept applies to the number of timesteps:
ems_option_set(n_timestep_header = "NINTERVAL")
Default values for these settings (and others) may be obtained using:
ems_option_get()

7.7.1 Leads, lags and parallel solving
In intertemporal models, the parallel matrix methods (see Solving the model) solve each period as a block, with the variables that link periods held in a shared border. Only the elements a lead or lag actually references join that border: qo("capital",r,t+1) adds the capital slice of qo and nothing else, and the solver’s log reports the border it found (Border netcut). A lead or lag on a whole variable declared over large sets (for example qo(c,r,t+1) over all commodities and regions) does enlarge the border and can remove the benefit of solving in parallel.
Link periods through a small proxy variable in that case:
Variable (all,r,REG)(all,t,ALLTIME)
    kb(r,t) # beginning-of-period capital stock #;
Equation E_kb
(all,r,REG)(all,t,ALLTIME)
    kb(r,t) = qo("capital",r,t);
and place the lead on the proxy (kb(r,t+1)). The vetted intertemporal models already follow this pattern.

title: 8  Closure swaps
text:
8.1 Overview
Swaps allow the user to reconfigure which variables are exogenous (provided by the modeler) and which are endogenous (solved by the model). Simple full variable swaps can be directly inputted as a string into the swap_in and swap_out arguments of ems_deploy(). More complex swaps must be handled with the dedicated ems_swap() function.

title: 8  Closure swaps
text:
8.2 Simple (full variable) swaps
Here, simple swaps refer to swaps in which a variable and all its components are being swapped. This is the most common type of swap and is directly handled within ems_deploy().
A single full variable swap:
cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  swap_in = "qfd",
  swap_out = "tfd"
)
Multiple full variable swaps:
cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  swap_in = c("qfd", "yp"),
  swap_out = c("tfd", "dppriv")
)
Swaps “in” and “out” are reconciled together rather than in a fixed order: each variable element ends exogenous or endogenous according to the net of the swaps that name it. A variable can therefore be swapped in whole and a slice of it swapped back out, and a swap followed by its mirror leaves the closure unchanged. Swaps are rejected only when no order of them is valid on the closure, for example when the same element is swapped in twice.

8.2.1 Choosing swaps
A closure must leave as many endogenous variable elements as there are equations, so every element swapped in needs an element swapped out; ems_deploy() aborts when a closure is invalid. Each pair should also make economic sense: the variable swapped out takes up the adjustment that the newly fixed variable no longer can. In the examples above, exogenous qfd with endogenous tfd fixes a firm’s demand for a domestic commodity and lets the tax on that purchase move to deliver it, the tax equivalent of a quantity target; a quota that may or may not bind needs a complementarity instead (Harrison et al. 2004). Exogenous yp with endogenous dppriv fixes private consumption expenditure and lets the distribution parameter of regional income adjust (Corong et al. 2017). Keep a price numeraire exogenous (pfactwld in the GTAP closures): the model determines relative prices only, and without one the price level is undetermined (Dixon et al. 1982).

title: 8  Closure swaps
text:
8.3 Complex (partial variable) swaps

8.3.1 ems_swap()
ems_swap() prepares a partial variable swap for use in the swap_in or swap_out arguments of ems_deploy(). Set arguments in ... use the model-specific set-index naming convention (set name concatenated with the variable’s index letter, e.g. REGr, ACTSa) to identify which tuples to include in the swap.
ems_swap(
  var,
  ...
)








Argument
Type
Description




var
Character
Variable name as it appears in the model file


...
Named arguments
Set-index pairs restricting the swap. Each value is a single element ("element"), multiple elements (c("a", "b")), or a named subset ("SUBSET")



Partial variable swaps entail swapping parts of a variable (i.e., subsets of the constitutive sets) and must be processed through the ems_swap() function. In the above example the full “qfd” and “yp” variables were made exogenous, while the full “tfd” and “dppriv” variables become endogenous. Within the GTAPv7 model, “qfd” encompasses the “COMM”, “ACTS”, and “REG” sets:
Variable (orig_level=VDFB)(all,c,COMM)(all,a,ACTS)(all,r,REG)
    qfd(c,a,r) # demand for domestic commodity c by activity a in region r #;
What if we wish to shock only certain parts of this variable (e.g., a region or commodity) and allow the remainder of the variable to endogenously adjust according to model equations? In this case we would swap on the parts of the variable that we will provide values to and leave the remainder. If, for example, we have a shock value for “asia” within “REG” and “crops” within “ACTS”, the following ems_swap() call will prepare this swap for input into the swap_in argument of ems_deploy():
qfd_in <- ems_swap(
  var = "qfd",
  REGr = "asia",
  ACTSa = "crops"
)
***Note that sets specified in this manner are identified by the model-specific concatenation of the standard set name plus the variable-specific index. This is necessary because many variables contain multiple instances of the same set and none of the teems functions relies upon input entry order or order within the model to make distinctions. In this case the “qfd” set subindices are “c”, “a”, and “r”, yielding “COMMc”, “ACTSa”, and “REGr”. In order to retain a valid closure we also use the same approach to the outgoing variable “tfd”:
tfd_out <- ems_swap(
  var = "tfd",
  REGr = "asia",
  ACTSa = "crops"
)
While the subindices for both variables are the same within GTAPv7, note that these may vary in some models such as GTAPv6 where the REG subindex is “s” for “qfd” and “r” for “tfd”. Both swaps may now be loaded within ems_deploy():
cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  swap_in = qfd_in,
  swap_out = tfd_out
)
Or if additional full variable swaps are also desired, a list is used to load multiple swaps for each direction:
cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  swap_in = list(qfd_in, "yp"),
  swap_out = list(tfd_out, "dppriv")
)
Finally, selection of multiple elements for each set will expand the swap to encompass all associated tuples. For example:
qfd_in <- ems_swap(
  var = "qfd",
  REGr = c("asia", "lam"),
  ACTSa = "crops"
)
is equivalent to loading
qfd_in_1 <- ems_swap(
  var = "qfd",
  REGr = "asia",
  ACTSa = "crops"
)
and
qfd_in_2 <- ems_swap(
  var = "qfd",
  REGr = "lam",
  ACTSa = "crops"
)


8.3.2 Subset swaps
A named model subset may be passed in place of individual elements. teems expands the subset to all its elements at the aggregation level specified in ems_data(). This is useful when a model defines meaningful groupings that map directly to closure logic such as margin commodities or forward time steps in intertemporal models.
In the GTAP-RE model, MARG is a subset of COMM containing margin commodities, and FWDTIME is a subset of ALLTIME containing forward time steps. Passing these subset names directly restricts the swap to only those elements:
qxs_in <- ems_swap(
  var = "qxs",
  COMMc = "MARG",
  REGs = c("chn", "usa"),
  ALLTIMEt = "FWDTIME"
)

txs_out <- ems_swap(
  var = "txs",
  COMMc = "MARG",
  REGs = c("chn", "usa"),
  ALLTIMEt = "FWDTIME"
)

cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  shock = partial,
  swap_in = qxs_in,
  swap_out = txs_out
)
Note that REGs = c("chn", "usa") is a multi-element specification, while COMMc = "MARG" and ALLTIMEt = "FWDTIME" are subset specifications. Both the above forms can be combined freely in a single ems_swap() call.

title: 9  Uniform shocks
text:
9.1 Overview
ems_uniform_shock() applies a homogeneous shock over an entire variable or a subset of its elements. The set arguments accepted in ... depend on the variable specified and the set mappings loaded in ems_data().

title: 9  Uniform shocks
text:
ems_uniform_shock(
  var,
  value,
  ...
)








Argument
Type
Description




var
Character
Variable name as it appears in the model file


value
Numeric
Shock applied to all targeted elements: a percentage change for a percent-change variable, an ordinary change for a change variable


...
Named arguments
Set-index pairs restricting the shock. Each value is a single element ("element"), multiple elements (c("a", "b")), or a named subset ("SUBSET")

title: 9  Uniform shocks
text:
9.2 Full variable uniform shocks
The simplest uniform shock is applied to a full variable, meaning that all combinations of sets associated with that variable are allocated the same exogenous value. In the example below, all regions (as determined by selected region mappings) will be increased by 1%.
pop_shk <- ems_uniform_shock(var = "pop",
                             value = 1
)

title: 9  Uniform shocks
text:
9.3 Partial variable uniform shocks
As with swaps, a uniform shock can be restricted to elements of the sets the variable is declared over, named by the set name concatenated with the variable’s index (REGr, ACTSa). To shock the region “chn” alone:
partial <- ems_uniform_shock(var = "aoall",
                             value = -1,
                             REGr = "chn"
)
Exogenous elements the shock does not name (here every region but “chn”) keep a zero change.
In an intertemporal model the time element may be given as a chronological year, Year = 2017, or as a time step through the time set (see the “Time step summary” that ems_data() prints):
partial <- ems_uniform_shock(
  var = "aoall",
  value = -1,
  REGr = "chn",
  ACTSa = "crops",
  Year = 2017
)

title: 9  Uniform shocks
text:
9.4 Subset shocks
A named model subset may be passed in place of individual elements, identical to the subset form in ems_swap(). teems expands the subset to all its elements at the aggregation level specified in ems_data().
In the GTAP-RE model, MARG is a subset of COMM containing margin commodities, and FWDTIME is a subset of ALLTIME containing forward time steps. Using these subset names directly restricts the shock to only those elements:
partial <- ems_uniform_shock(
  var = "qxs",
  value = -1,
  COMMc = "MARG",
  REGs = c("chn", "usa"),
  ALLTIMEt = "FWDTIME"
)
As in the swaps example, REGs = c("chn", "usa") is a multi-element specification while COMMc = "MARG" and ALLTIMEt = "FWDTIME" are subset specifications. This shock would then be deployed alongside the corresponding subset swaps:
cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  shock = partial,
  swap_in = qxs_in,
  swap_out = txs_out
)

title: 9  Uniform shocks
10  Custom shocks
text:
10.1 Overview
ems_custom_shock() allows for heterogeneous shocks specified on a tuple-by-tuple basis, supplied as a data frame or CSV file through input. Values are percentage changes for percent-change variables and ordinary changes for change variables. Only the tuples present in input are shocked.

title: 10  Custom shocks
text:
ems_custom_shock(
  var,
  input
)








Argument
Type
Description




var
Character
Variable name as it appears in the model file


input
Data frame or Character
Data frame or path to a CSV file containing set columns and a Value column (the shock in the variable’s own form)

title: 10  Custom shocks
text:
10.2 Full variable custom shocks
Custom shocks can be carried out over the full variable, with every tuple receiving a specified shock value. Here is a demonstration of 4 custom shocks carried out on all variable tuples for a range of variable dimensions with the GTAP-RE model.
Elements for data frame construction
time_steps <- c(0, 1, 2, 3)
REG <- c("chn", "usa", "row")
ENDW <- c("labor", "capital", "natlres", "land")
COMM <- c("svces", "food", "crops", "mnfcs", "livestock")
ACTS <- COMM
MARG <- "svces"
ALLTIME <- seq(0, length(time_steps) - 1)
2D data frame and shock
pop <- expand.grid(
  REGr = REG,
  ALLTIMEt = ALLTIME,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

pop <- pop[do.call(order, pop), ]
pop$Value <- runif(nrow(pop))

pop_shk <- ems_custom_shock(
  var = "pop",
  input = pop
)
3D data frame and shock
aoall <- expand.grid(
  ACTSa = ACTS,
  REGr = REG,
  ALLTIMEt = ALLTIME,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

aoall <- aoall[do.call(order, aoall), ]
aoall$Value <- runif(nrow(aoall))

aoall_shk <- ems_custom_shock(
  var = "aoall",
  input = aoall
)
4D data frame and shock
afeall <- expand.grid(
  ENDWe = ENDW,
  ACTSa = ACTS,
  REGr = REG,
  ALLTIMEt = ALLTIME,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

afeall <- afeall[do.call(order, afeall), ]
afeall$Value <- runif(nrow(afeall))

afeall_shk <- ems_custom_shock(
  var = "afeall",
  input = afeall
)
5D data frame and shock
atall <- expand.grid(
  MARGm = MARG,
  COMMc = COMM,
  REGs = REG,
  REGd = REG,
  ALLTIMEt = ALLTIME,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

atall <- atall[do.call(order, atall), ]
atall$Value <- runif(nrow(atall))

atall_shk <- ems_custom_shock(
  var = "atall",
  input = atall
)
Multiple custom shocks are combined in a list for ems_deploy():
cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  shock = list(pop_shk, aoall_shk, afeall_shk, atall_shk)
)

title: 10  Custom shocks
text:
10.3 CSV input
A path to a CSV file can be passed to input instead of a data frame. The CSV must follow the same structure: one column per set index using the model-specific naming convention and a Value column. Column order is inconsequential.
pop_csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(pop, pop_csv, row.names = FALSE)

pop_shk <- ems_custom_shock(
  var = "pop",
  input = pop_csv
)

title: 10  Custom shocks
text:
10.4 Partial variable custom shocks
Custom shocks are only carried out on tuples included within the input data frame or CSV. Here we carry out a custom shock (heterogenous values) across part of the aoall variable. The non-shocked values will remain at 0 due to their exogenous status.
aoall_full <- expand.grid(
  ACTSa = ACTS,
  REGr = REG,
  ALLTIMEt = ALLTIME,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
aoall_full$Value <- 0
aoall_full <- aoall_full[do.call(order, aoall_full), ]
aoall <- aoall_full[
  !(aoall_full$ACTSa == "crops" & aoall_full$REGr == "usa") &
  aoall_full$ALLTIMEt != 3,
]
aoall$Value <- runif(nrow(aoall))
aoall_shk  <- ems_custom_shock(var = "aoall",  input = aoall)

title: 10  Custom shocks
text:
10.5 Chronological year input
For intertemporal models, the time dimension can be specified using chronological years instead of integer time steps by using a Year column in place of ALLTIMEt. The year values must correspond to the reference year and steps defined in ems_data().
time_steps <- c(2017, 2018, 2019, 2020)

dat <- ems_data(
  dat_input = dat_input,
  par_input = par_input,
  set_input = set_input,
  time_steps = time_steps,
  REG = "big3",
  ACTS = "macro_sector",
  ENDW = "labor_agg"
)
Construct the input data frame with a Year column rather than ALLTIMEt:
REG <- c("chn", "usa", "row")

pop <- expand.grid(
  REGr = REG,
  Year = time_steps,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

pop <- pop[do.call(order, pop), ]
pop$Value <- runif(nrow(pop))

pop_shk <- ems_custom_shock(
  var = "pop",
  input = pop
)
With ems_custom_shock(), a Year column is recognized automatically and mapped to the corresponding integer time step internally.

title: 11  Scenario shocks
text:
11.1 Overview
ems_scenario_shock() is an intertemporal shock type that specifies heterogeneous shocks at the tuple level as absolute values. By default, inputs must cover all pre-aggregation tuples and span the full extent of the variable; with partial = TRUE they may cover only some of the aggregated tuples (see Partial scenario shocks). Values must be in the same units as the underlying database coefficient; at deployment they are summed over the set mappings of ems_data(), and each year’s aggregated value becomes the percentage change from the base-year value (the ordinary change for a variable declared (change)), so the same input serves any aggregation.

title: 11  Scenario shocks
text:
ems_scenario_shock(
  var,
  input,
  partial = FALSE
)








Argument
Type
Description

Character
Variable name as it appears in the model file


input
Data frame or Character
Data frame or path to a CSV file containing all pre-aggregation tuples, a Year column (chronological years), and a Value column (absolute values)

Logical
If TRUE, input may cover only some aggregated tuples; only those are shocked (default FALSE)

title: 11  Scenario shocks
text:
11.2 Using scenario shocks
Scenario shocks differ from custom shocks in a number of respects:

Only available for intertemporal models
Inputs must contain all preaggregation tuples associated with a variable, unless partial = TRUE
Inputs are denominated in absolute values in the units of the underlying database coefficient (e.g., million $USD, population)
The input data frame or CSV must contain a Year column of chronological years, the base year included, since each later year’s shock is the change from the base-year value

There are several applications where it is advantageous to use scenario shock rather than a custom shock. The primary advantage is that scenario shocks allow for seamless changes to model aggregations since the shocks themselves are subject to mappings and aggregation. If we have trajectories available for all tuples within a given variable, a scenario shock will adjust to set mapping inputs in ems_data(). Because values are summed over the pre-aggregation tuples before the percentage change is taken, they must be levels in common real units (e.g., persons, million USD). Index values such as a base of 1 for every country would give an aggregated region the unweighted mean of its members’ growth rather than their size-weighted growth; they are safe only when no tuple is aggregated.

title: 11  Scenario shocks
text:
11.3 Population trajectory example
Here is an example that takes base year population data from the GTAP database (typically not read into the model) and constructs hypothetical pathways for every region in the model. These pathways are valid for any regional aggregation chosen.
Set up the model run with chronological time steps:
year <- 2017
time_steps <- year + c(0, 1, 2, 3)

dat <- ems_data(
  dat_input = "v7_data/gsdfdat.har",
  par_input = "v7_data/gsdfpar.har",
  set_input = "v7_data/gsdfset.har",
  time_steps = time_steps,
  REG = "big3",
  ACTS = "macro_sector",
  ENDW = "labor_agg"
)

GTAP_RE <- ems_example("GTAP-RE", tempdir())
model <- ems_model(
  model_file = GTAP_RE[["model_file"]],
  closure_file = GTAP_RE[["closure_file"]]
)
Load POP at full regional resolution (unaggregated) as the scenario baseline. The REG = "full" call does not require time_steps since it is only used to extract the base-year coefficient:
pop <- ems_data(
  dat_input = "v7_data/gsdfdat.har",
  par_input = "v7_data/gsdfpar.har",
  set_input = "v7_data/gsdfset.har",
  REG = "full",
  ACTS = "macro_sector",
  ENDW = "labor_agg"
)$POP
Construct trajectories with compound growth through each future time step. tail(time_steps, -1) yields the forward time steps, keeping the trajectory in sync with whatever time_steps was passed to ems_data():
pop$Year <- year
regions <- unique(pop$REG)

pop_traj <- expand.grid(REG = regions, Year = tail(time_steps, -1),
                        stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
pop_traj$Value <- 0
pop <- rbind(pop, pop_traj)

set.seed(42)
growth_rates <- data.frame(
  REG = regions,
  growth_rate = runif(length(regions), min = -0.01, max = 0.05)
)

pop <- merge(pop, growth_rates, by = "REG")
base_values <- pop[pop$Year == year, c("REG", "Value")]
names(base_values)[2] <- "base_value"
pop <- merge(pop, base_values, by = "REG")

pop$Value[pop$Year > year] <-
  pop$base_value[pop$Year > year] *
    (1 + pop$growth_rate[pop$Year > year])^(pop$Year[pop$Year > year] - year)

pop$growth_rate <- NULL
pop$base_value <- NULL
pop <- pop[order(pop$REG, pop$Year), c("REG", "Year", "Value")]
ems_data() returns coefficients with plain set names (e.g., REG). Rename to the model’s set-index convention before passing to ems_scenario_shock():
colnames(pop)[colnames(pop) == "REG"] <- "REGr"
Pass pop as the scenario shock and deploy:
pop_trajectory <- ems_scenario_shock(
  var = "pop",
  input = pop
)

cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  shock = pop_trajectory
)
pop may also be saved as a CSV and loaded directly by passing the file path to input.

title: 11  Scenario shocks
text:
11.4 Partial scenario shocks
Sometimes trajectories exist for only part of a variable, for example the population of a single region. With partial = TRUE, a scenario shock covers only the aggregated tuples its input fully supplies. Every pre-aggregation tuple that maps to a shocked aggregated tuple must be present, in every year. An aggregated tuple that is only partly covered stops the deployment by name, because the percentage change of a partial sum is not the change of the whole group.
Continuing the example above, the following shocks population in the United States and China only, which are their own regions in the "big3" aggregation:
pop_partial <- pop[pop$REGr %in% c("usa", "chn"), ]

cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  shock = ems_scenario_shock(var = "pop", input = pop_partial, partial = TRUE)
)
The shocked tuples must be exogenous, and exogenous tuples outside the input keep a zero change. The same input stops under an aggregation that groups the United States with other countries, unless those countries are supplied as well. Since values are summed over the pre-aggregation tuples, scenario shocks, partial or not, suit additive variables such as values and quantities.

title: 12  Deploying the model
text:
12.1 Overview
ems_deploy() validates all data and model inputs, processes shocks and closure swaps, and writes all required input files to disk. The output file path serves as a required input to ems_solve().

  .data,
  model,
  shock = NULL,
  swap_in = NULL,
  swap_out = NULL,
  shock_file = NULL,
  write_coefficients = FALSE

title: 12  Deploying the model
text:
12.3 Basic usage
The simplest deployment requires only data and model inputs. With no shock supplied, input data is returned without change:
cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model
)

title: 12  Deploying the model
text:
12.4 Deploying with shocks and swaps
A single shock can be passed directly:
shock <- ems_uniform_shock(var = "pop", value = 1)

cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  shock = shock
)
Multiple shocks are combined in a list:
pop_shk <- ems_uniform_shock(var = "pop", value = 1)
aoall_shk <- ems_custom_shock(var = "aoall", input = aoall_df)

cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  shock = list(pop_shk, aoall_shk)
)

title: 12  Deploying the model
text:
12.5 Closure swaps
A single full variable swap swaps one variable in and one out using plain strings:
shock <- ems_uniform_shock(var = "qfd", value = 1)

cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  shock = shock,
  swap_in = "qfd",
  swap_out = "tfd"
)
Multiple full variable swaps are passed as character vectors. Partial swaps use ems_swap() objects and can be mixed with strings in a list:
# Multiple full variable swaps
cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  shock = shock,
  swap_in = c("qfd", "yp"),
  swap_out = c("tfd", "dppriv")
)

# Mixed partial and full swaps
yp_row <- ems_swap("yp", REGr = "row")
dppriv_row <- ems_swap("dppriv", REGr = "row")

cmf_path <- ems_deploy(
  .data = dat,
  model = model,
  shock = shock,
  swap_in = list(yp_row, "qfd"),
  swap_out = list(dppriv_row, "tfd")
)

title: 12  Deploying the model
text:
12.6 User-generated inputs
ems_deploy() allows for user-generated shock files via the shock_file argument. In the case of shock files, no checks or operations will be conducted (i.e., the shock file as loaded is considered the final input). User-supplied closure files will however be processed if swaps are supplied.

title: 13  Solving the model
text:
13.1 Overview
ems_solve() runs the teems solver on a deployed model and, by default, parses the results into structured R objects with ems_compose(). A teems Docker image must be available. After the run, the solve is checked for singularity, accuracy and errors, and the findings are written to model_diagnostics.txt in the run directory. On Linux the solver container runs as the calling user, so the files it writes to the run directory belong to you.
ems_solve() chooses nothing on your behalf: the run is exactly the arguments given, so it can be reproduced from its record. A bare ems_solve(cmf_path) solves with Gragg 2-4-6 (as GEMPACK) and LU on one task and one thread, which is accurate and correct for every model but slow for large ones. ems_probe() suggests what to use instead.

title: 13  Solving the model
text:
ems_solve(
  cmf_path,
  solution_method = c("Gragg", "Johansen", "Euler", "Midpoint", "RK2",
                      "Heun", "RK4", "BoSha32", "DoPri54"),
  matrix_method = c("LU", "DBBD", "SBBD", "NDBBD"),
  n_subintervals = 1L,
  steps = NULL,
  n_tasks = 1L,
  n_threads = 1L,
  precision = c("single", "double"),
  verbosity = 1L,
  suppress_outputs = FALSE,
  terminal_run = FALSE,
  accuracy_vars = NULL,
  ...
)

text:
13.2 Basic usage
outputs <- ems_solve(
  cmf_path = cmf_path,
  solution_method = "Gragg",
  matrix_method = "LU"
)

title: 13  Solving the model
text:
13.4 Solution methods



Method
Use it for




"Gragg"
The default and the standard accurate method: several multi-step solutions combined by extrapolation (see the GEMPACK manual)


"Johansen"
A quick one-step linear approximation. Good for checking that a model and closure run; not accurate for nonlinear results or large shocks


"Euler"
Like "Gragg" but converges more slowly. With adaptive "DoPri54" or "BoSha32", the choice for severe shocks, such as a variable driven close to -100%, where "Gragg" and "Midpoint" can become unstable (GEMPACK manual 30.2; Schiffmann 2022)


"Midpoint"
Gragg’s method without its final smoothing pass. It never carries the shocks past their end point, so it takes a shock of exactly -100%, which "Gragg" refuses


"RK2", "Heun", "RK4"
Runge-Kutta methods with a single step count and no extrapolation. "RK4" with a few steps is an inexpensive way to get three to four correct digits on large shocks


"BoSha32", "DoPri54"
Runge-Kutta methods that estimate their own error and can control their step size (adaptive = "yes")



"Gragg" suits most work; "Johansen" is a quicker way to check that a new setup runs, and adaptive "DoPri54" is an alternative for large shocks. A shock that is too large for the step schedule shows up as a singularity abort preceded by warnings that updated coefficients crossed their declared bounds; ems_solve() then names the remedies below rather than the closure. On large shocks, use more than one subinterval with "Gragg":
outputs <- ems_solve(
  cmf_path = cmf_path,
  solution_method = "Gragg",
  n_subintervals = 4,
  steps = c(2, 4, 8)
)
With matrix_method = "DBBD", a run split into subintervals can occasionally abort with a singularity partway through the shock although the closure is sound; the solver names the elements involved. Change n_subintervals (1 is the simplest) or use matrix_method = "LU" for that run.
Adaptive "DoPri54" reaches about the same accuracy with roughly half the work. It controls its own step size, so n_subintervals does not apply, and it returns a per-element error_estimate column. Treat the estimate as a pointer to the least settled results, not as a bound on the error.
outputs <- ems_solve(
  cmf_path = cmf_path,
  solution_method = "DoPri54",
  steps = 4,
  adaptive = "yes",
  eps_tolerance = 0.01
)
outputs$dat$qgdp$error_estimate
To check that a result has converged, repeat the run with a tighter eps_tolerance or more steps and compare. The finer Runge-Kutta controls are described below.

13.4.1 Step counts and single-pass runs
"Gragg", "Midpoint" and "Euler" normally solve three times with increasing step counts and extrapolate from the three results, which also gives the accuracy summary. The summary covers every endogenous result unless accuracy_vars names the variables it should cover, for example accuracy_vars = c("qgdp", "pm"). The "Gragg" and "Midpoint" counts must be all even or all odd (c(2, 4, 6) or c(3, 5, 7)); even counts are recommended. Two counts (c(2, 4)) extrapolate from two results, with no accuracy summary. The package option converge = TRUE applies GEMPACK’s treatment of results that do not converge cleanly: their extrapolation is replaced by the result with the most steps, or by the average when the three results are nearly equal.
A single count gives one multi-step run without extrapolation:
outputs <- ems_solve(
  cmf_path = cmf_path,
  solution_method = "Euler",
  steps = 16
)
Use it for models whose updated data must follow the steps themselves, such as a step counter or an iterative (RAS-style) balancing update, which extrapolation would distort. No accuracy summary is available for a single-pass run.


13.4.2 Runge-Kutta controls
ems_RK(
  cmf_path,
  solution_method = c("DoPri54", "BoSha32", "RK4", "Heun", "RK2"),
  steps = 4L,
  eps_tolerance = 0.01,
  adaptive = NULL,
  matrix_method = c("LU", "DBBD", "SBBD", "NDBBD"),
  n_tasks = 1L,
  n_threads = 1L,
  precision = c("single", "double"),
  n_subintervals = 1L,
  verbosity = 1L,
  suppress_outputs = FALSE,
  terminal_run = FALSE,
  accuracy_vars = NULL,
  max_retries = 3L,
  retry_adjust = 0.5,
  chart = c("log", "percent"),
  error_norm = c("max", "rms"),
  controller = c("std", "pi"),
  scope = c("pct", "all"),
  h_init = NULL,
  guard = NULL,
  ...
)
ems_RK() is ems_solve() for the Runge-Kutta methods. It defaults to adaptive "DoPri54" and adds the step-size controls; the remaining arguments are those of ems_solve(), with the same defaults. When most retries come from step checks (a variable approaching -100%, a range test) rather than from eps_tolerance, the cheaper steps of "BoSha32" can make it faster than "DoPri54" (Schiffmann 2022).
# adaptive DoPri54
outputs <- ems_RK(cmf_path)

# fixed-step RK4
outputs <- ems_RK(cmf_path, solution_method = "RK4", steps = 8L)

title: 13  Solving the model
text:
13.5 Matrix methods








Method
Models
Description




"LU"
all
Sequential LU factorization. The most robust; one task only


"DBBD"
static
Splits the system into blocks (usually by region) solved in parallel, treating regions as separable economies (Kompas and Van Ha 2019)


"SBBD"

Splits the system by time period, solved in parallel (Van Ha and Kompas 2016; Van Ha et al. 2017)

A nested split for intertemporal models too large for "SBBD" in the available memory




13.5.1 Choosing a method and resources
ems_probe(
  cmf_path,
  components = TRUE,
  cores = NULL,
  memory = NULL,
  ...
)
Run ems_probe() once per deployment, before the first solve. It runs the solver up to the point where the equation system is assembled, without solving, and from that system it checks that the closure is sound, measures the structure the matrix methods exploit, reads the cores and memory available to the solver’s container, and prints the call to use. A probe takes seconds on a condensed GTAP model; on an uncondensed system its cost grows faster than the size, to minutes at a few million equations.
probe <- ems_probe(cmf_path)
#> ℹ Probing 'GTAPv7.cmf'; solver log at 'out/probe/solver_out_probe.txt'
#> ℹ Probe finished in 20.9 s
probe
#> ── Structural probe ─────────────────────────────────── 110,849 equations ──
#> ✔ Closure valid: every variable is determined and no equation is redundant,
#>   structurally and at base data
#> → Recommended for this container (8 cores, 12.0 GB): "LU", 1 task × 8
#>   threads
#>   `ems_solve(cmf_path, matrix_method = "LU", n_threads = 8)`
#> ℹ `summary(x)` for the full report
Pass cores and memory (in GB) to get the recommendation for another machine, for example a server you will solve on later.
ems_probe() is experimental. Its rules come from a limited set of measured models and machines, so treat the recommendation as a starting point: a different method, task count or thread count may well be faster for your model and machine. Try other settings with ems_solve(), and if a suggestion is off, please open an issue.

13.5.1.1 Reading the printed summary
While it runs, the two progress lines name the deployment, the solver log and the time taken; any Warning: lines the solver wrote to that log are repeated afterwards. Both are silent under ems_option_set(verbose = FALSE). The short form printed above has four parts:

The header gives the number of equations in the system the solver will factorize. For a condensed model (the vetted static models) this is the system after backsolving, which is much smaller than the model.
The closure verdict. Closure valid means that every endogenous variable is pinned down by some equation and no equation duplicates another, both in the model’s structure and with the base data in place. A model that fails this test cannot be solved, however it is configured; the alternative lines are described under Singular systems.
A memory warning, only when the estimated peak of the recommended run comes close to the container’s memory.
The recommendation: the matrix method, the number of parallel tasks and the threads per task, for the machine named in brackets, followed by the ems_solve() call to paste. “This container” means the cores and memory were read from the Docker container the solver runs in (on Docker Desktop, the limits under Settings > Resources); “the machine given” means you passed cores and memory.

When no sound recommendation can be made, the probe says so instead of guessing: the closure is singular (fix the model first), the container’s cores could not be read (pass cores and memory), or no method fits in the memory available (the message gives the smallest estimate and the remedies: more memory for the container, a coarser aggregation, or condensation).
